problem: The bullet 'H=1 bit is the maximum for two balanced classes' can be misread. The maximum over all two-class distributions is 1 bit; balance is the condition that achieves it, not a restriction on the maximum.
fix: H is at most 1 bit when there are two classes. It reaches exactly 1 bit when the classes are split 50-50.

where: Section 3, recursion steps and Section 2 formula
problem: Neither the gain formula nor the recursion says what happens when some value v of the chosen attribute has no examples (Sv empty). Then H(Sv) is undefined and the child node cannot be built, which a student can hit with sparse data such as a Weather value that no training day has.
fix: Add: if Sv is empty, give that branch weight 0 in the gain sum (skip its entropy term) and make the branch a leaf labelled with the majority class of S.

problem: 'A high-branch attribute' is unclear wording; students will not know whether it means an attribute high in the tree or one with many branches.
fix: An attribute with many values can get high gain just by having many values.

problem: 'base 10 gives different numbers, though ranking can be the same' understates the fact. Changing the log base multiplies every information gain by the same positive constant 1/log₂10, so the ranking of attributes is always identical at every node and the tree built is the same.
fix: Use log₂ and bits in this syllabus; base 10 gives numbers smaller by the factor 1/log₂10 ≈ 0.301, but because every gain is scaled by the same constant, the attribute ranking and the resulting tree are identical.
